extracted.intended_audience: playwrights/dramatic_writers, actors, and literate readers interested in drama and conduct
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive guidance and critical standards for composing and judging English tragedy (style, metre, plot, character, endings, and performance), together with related social-conduct advice (avoidance of affectation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate reading for women's improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommend such particular Books as may be proper for the Improvement of the Sex; books that have a Tendency to enlighten the Understanding and rectify the Passions, as well as those which divert the Imagination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author proposes to publish another paper recommending particular books and invites correspondents' thoughts. Implicit guidance: prefer books that enlighten understanding and correct passions over merely diverting works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and signs of Affectation
rubrics_metrics.description: Affectation arises when Consciousness is employed in too fondly approving a person's own conceptions; every second thought betrays an Interruption and shows itself in gestures, looks, words, and posture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given: exaggerated laughter, pose-making to display a limb, adjusted dress and discomposure after a failed affectation. Affectation is detectable in both trivial and distinguished characters (men and women).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding Affectation (remedies)
rubrics_metrics.description: To rid oneself of the desire for praise (affectation), fix the heart on the main design of life and be thoroughly indifferent in small particulars; throw off the love of praise upon occasions that are not laudable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical advice from the text: be indifferent where praise is not due; allow no man to praise you to your face (so your vanity 'will want its food'); cultivate being praised by actions rather than compliments; concentrate on great virtues rather than little perfections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on chief purpose to avoid small-perfection anxiety
rubrics_metrics.description: When thoughts are employed upon the chief purpose in business or pleasure, one will not betray affectation; fear of erring in indifferent things argues an over-valuation of small merits and robs capacity for great things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Antipattern: being oppressed about minor ways of speaking or acting; remedy: fix heart on one point and judge nothing an error except what deviates from that intention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blank verse preferred over rhyme for English tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Blank verse is the most proper for Tragedy in English; a Play in Rhyme is as absurd in English as a Tragedy in Hexameters would be in Greek or Latin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not mix Scenes in Rhyme and Scenes in Blank Verse (they become two different languages). Exception: can conclude a Tragedy, or every Act, with two or three couplets (like an air after recitativo) to give an actor a graceful exit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use diversity of numbers and hemistichs to vary modulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce diversity of numbers (meters) and half-verses (hemistichs) in order to prevent the ear from being tired and to suit expressed passions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abrupt pauses, breakings-off in the middle of a verse, and hemistichs are permissible and effective when they humour or express a passion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer noble thought over sonorous but common sense
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer a noble Sentiment that is depressed with homely Language infinitely before a vulgar one that is blown up with all the Sound and Energy of Expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diagnosis: English poets often succeed in style but fail in sentiments — language may be noble and sonorous while sense is trifling. Remedy: lay down the naked thought in plain English before versifying, and readers should judge the thought divested of tragic ornaments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Labour expression in unactive parts; keep passion-language simple
rubrics_metrics.description: Expression ought to be very much laboured in the unactive Parts of the Fable (descriptions, similitudes, narrations), because opinions, manners and passions are apt to be obscured by pompous phrases and elaborate expressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guided by Aristotle: elaborate language belongs in descriptive/unemotional passages; in representing passions, avoid pompous phrases that obscure the thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not obscure great thoughts with sounding phrases or hard metaphors
rubrics_metrics.description: Great and just thoughts are often obscured by sounding Phrases, hard Metaphors, and forced Expressions in which they are clothed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example critique of Shakespeare: fine thoughts lost in a cloud of words. Practical step: consider the naked thought of every speech when divested of tragic ornaments to judge its naturalness and appropriateness for the person who utters it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrain impetuosity; ease the style to reveal thought
rubrics_metrics.description: Poets with impetuous genius (e.g., Lee) should restrain and keep within proper bounds; simplicity and easing the style can reveal natural beauty in passion and description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Lee's thoughts are suited to Tragedy but often lost in word-cloud; Otway follows nature in language and therefore shines in passionate parts. Remedy: slacken efforts where necessary and avoid an overabundance of epithets and metaphors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy need not enforce poetic justice; unhappy endings are effective
rubrics_metrics.description: English writers wrongly assume they must deliver virtue out of troubles; there is no foundation for equal distribution of rewards and punishments — tragedies that end unhappily often please and produce stronger terror and commiseration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle observed that tragedies which ended unhappily pleased the people and carried away the prize. Examples of successful unhappy-ended plays: The Orphan, Venice Preserved, King Lear (originally). The caution: do not establish happy resolution as the only method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid Tragi-Comedy and unrelated double plots
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragi-Comedy (mixing mirth and sorrow) is absurd and double plots divert the audience's grief, breaking the tide of sorrow and weakening the principal action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an under-plot is used, it should bear a near relation to the principal design and be concluded by the same Catastrophe to preserve unity and impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'Rants' and bombast — vehemence should not substitute for thought
rubrics_metrics.description: Rants are warm and passionate parts where actors pronounce inflated language, adding vehemence where there was no passion, inflaming real passion into fustian; unnatural exclamations, curses, vows, blasphemies and defiance often pass for towering thoughts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Antipattern: actors and audiences applaud bombast (Powell raised applause by this artifice). Consequence: mouths of heroes filled with bombast rather than true greatness. Watch for lines that gain thunderous applause despite being less natural than quieter, more moving passages (example: OEdipus scene comparison).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not write merely to pander to an audience's taste for vehemence
rubrics_metrics.description: Some poets and actors practise insolent behaviour toward men and abject behaviour toward women on stage to win the favor of the boxes; authors should avoid shaping characters merely to please such tastes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warning: the fair part of the audience enjoys seeing a man insult kings or affront the gods in one scene and throw himself at his mistress in another. Such tailoring of character undermines true art and creates false favorites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of simile, description and ornament should be proportional to function
rubrics_metrics.description: Elaborate expression and ornamentation are appropriate where the fable is unactive (descriptions, similitudes, narrations); in parts representing opinions, manners and passions, excessive ornament tends to obscure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow Aristotle/Horace guidance: move laboured style into descriptive passages while keeping the expression of passions more direct and natural. Examples and footnotes reference classical authority.
